content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper is about training detectors using both real and synthetic data. The main contribution is it proposes to gradually transform and add a subset of synthetic images to the training set (real images). In each iteration, it selects a subset of synthetic images according to the `domain gap' using the pre-trained detector. Those synthetic images are then transformed using CycleGAN and added to the training set of the detector. Results show its performance improvement against several baseline methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength.
1. Methods are clearly written. Results show improvement against baseline methods. The idea of selecting `easy-to-transform' images seems interesting and inspiring.


Weaknesses
(Major) 
1. Lacks comparison to other domain adaption methods.  The proposed method is compared to methods that either use the all original synthetic data or all transformed data, in a fully supervised manner. The baseline methods are somehow `weak'.  There exist many other methods utilizing synthetic data, (or addressing the domain shift problem). i.e, adversarial domain adaption.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written and contains enough information for it to be reproduced.

Regarding novelty, the idea of modeling synthetic data training problems as curriculum learning by gradually adding `easy-to-transform' images is interesting, while other technical parts are more or less borrowed from existing work.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the idea of gradually transforming `easy' images is interesting, however, it lacks comparison to other domain adaption methods (e.g., adversarial domain adaption).  The idea is not fully evaluated yet.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a method to improve the performance of object detection fromUAV-based images by leveraging synthetic training data. Instead of simply combining the synthetic data with real data all at once, this paper proposes a scheme called Progressive Transformation Learning (PTL). To deal with the domain gap, PTL iteratively adds transformed synthetic images to the training set. In each iteration, a fixed number of synthetic images are sampled based on their Mahalanobis distances to the current training set. Experiment results on benchmark datasets show that the proposed scheme outperforms several baselines on few-shot learning for object detection and cross-domain detection.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ The paper is well written and easy to follow. The technical method, experiment setting and results are described clearly.
- The main idea of this paper is to use Progressive Transformation Learning when augmenting the training set with synthetic images. And PTL is based on measuring the domain gap using the Mahalanobis distances proposed in [Lee et al., 2018]. However, the benefits of the idea is not well justified. As mentioned in the paper, samples with larger domain gaps (i.e., out-of-distribution samples) are valuable because they increase the diversity of training set. So it is unclear to me whether preferring samples with smaller domain gap is an effective strategy. Also as shown in Table 2, the choice of \tau has little impact on the performance. Thus, one may guess that using random sampling on the synthetic data would also work well.
- It is shown in Table 1 that PTL outperforms several baselines. However, I wonder if the performance gain is actually due to iterative adding synthetic images (so that the synthetic data would not dominate the training), instead of the specific sampling strategy.
- The baselines compared in the paper are somewhat week. It would be better if more advanced domain adaption methods are considered.
- In Section 3.2, it is argued that the virtual2real transformation should not be applied to the cropped people region. In my opinion, this is not quite reasonable because the background provides important contextual information in object detection, especially for deep learning methods.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Overall, the paper is well organized and easy to follow.

Novelty is limited. The measure of domain gap is borrowed from [Lee et al., 2018], and the virtual2real transformation is based on CycleGAN.

In terms of reproducibility, detailed description of network design and hyper-parameters is missing. This paper does not mention if code and data will be released.
content.summary_of_the_review: As discussed above, I am not convinced that selecting synthetic images based on the domain gap is an effective strategy. Some method design choices are not well justified. Comparison with domain adaptation methods is missing.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The desire for large-scale datasets to train object detector is greater for object categories with more diverse appearances. Synthesizing virtual images to imitate real-world images is an intuitive way to expand the training set. Previous work can be summarized into three approaches:
1. Use virtual images to pre-trian a model and fine-tune the pre-trained model on real images.
2. Exploit additional information that can be easily labeled on  virtual images.
3. Directly build training batches consisting of both virtual images and real images.
The fisrt one avoid the domain gap between virtual images and real images while others don't handle at all. All these methods perform poor or even worse than training directly on real images.
This paper proposes a method that use virtual images to expand real image datasets by PTL:
1. measure the domain gap between real and virtual images.
2. choose virtual images by weighted random sampling.
3. transform the selected virtual images to real images by virtual2real transformation.
4. add the transformed images into real image set and remove the original images from virtual image set.
5. repeat 2~4 several times.
After PTL the real image set are largely expanded and can be used for downstream task.
Experiments show the distribution of the candidate selection and the accuracy variation as PTL evolves, results on low-shot learning and cross-domain detection accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. This paper measures the domain gap between virtual and real images. Select candidate virtual images with small gap and rarely appeared appreances together.
2. Virtual images can be conveniently and largely acquired to expand real image dataset.

Weakness:
1. Not novel enough, though applying PTL in leverage virtual images to expand real image datasets is a nice try.
2. The method of weighted random sampling is naive, as the experiments show the detection accracy is not sensitive to τ.
3. Why only select a pre-defined number of transformation candidates instead of a number x computed from the domain gap value. (Maybe this can handle domain gap and avoid iteration together).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clarity and quality are good to me.
content.summary_of_the_review: Please refer the strength and weakness part and I think the novelty of this paper is hard to reach the ICLR bar.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
